utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're starting rather late due to some problems, construction problems, apparently, that were taking place at the Detention Unit, and we will ask that in future we start at 9.00. For the rest of the day, we will take the normal breaks, but we'll go on sitting until 2.00, to try and make up time. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, we left off before the weekend break discussing a report by the command of the 9th Corps. I think we can read it out in open session without jeopardising your protective measures for this witness. Because I'm only going to ask him whether what it states in the document is correct or not. I'm not going to go into any other details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps I can be reminded where we'll find that. Have we got that? I think there was a report which was being dealt with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We started discussing the document just before we broke. It is the 20th of February, 1992 report of the 9th Corps, and it relates to the state of affairs in Krajina, the referendums, and other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a very long report, but I'm just going to look at certain passages and quotations for the witness to be able to answer. He can give simple yes or no answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll see how we get on, if you would like to start asking questions about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm going to quote from the document. The passage is brief, from page 1 of the report, and it talks about the fact that a referendum was announced for the United Nations Peace Plan, and under point 1, that it should be adopted, along with proposals and recommendations by the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, and that it should follow the lines of Vance's plan completely. And then we come to what it states further: The concept of Babic's and Vance's concepts in the leaflet, most of voters who are not fully informed of the developments, brings us into a situation that when we look at the leaflet at first glance, the voters reject the B variation and give full support to the first option. On the other hand, all the citizens of Krajina unconditionally advocate peace and the arrival of the Blue Helmets. So the referendum posters introduce -- baffle the people so that the people no longer know who to believe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question for this witness is as follows: Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the assessment of the person who wrote the report. The situation was that as of the month of November 1991, and then all through December and January and into February, the stands were published, made public, the stands of the government and assembly of the RSK, first of all the government, that is to say, and the assembly of the SAO Krajina, what the stand points were and positions with regard to the Cyrus Vance Peace Plan and what requests were made for the plan to be modified. The referendum was planned -- they planned to hold a referendum, but it wasn't put into practice because of the obstructions by the authorities that you yourself established, and the commands of the units of the JNA. The well known example is that of Stojan Spanovic, who was the commander of the brigade, who did not permit that the Cyrus Vance Plan be expounded and explained to the public along with the proposals for its modifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go on, the document has been traced. It is Exhibit D59, not yet translated. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The passage I read out states that the leaflets introduce confusion, so that the public no longer knows how to act. So my question is: Is that correct or is what you just said correct, when you said that the army and some kind of authorities from Belgrade did not allow them to state their views?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people didn't have an occasion to discuss this publicly under those conditions, nor to state their views about the plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. You said a moment ago that you had the positions of the government and the Assembly. However, in this same report, on page 2, it says the following: "In Glina, on the 16th of February," that is to say, four days prior to the publication of this report, "an assembly of the RSK was held under the --" The Presiding Officer was Mile Paspalj. I assume he was president of the Assembly at that time. And it made the decision to release Milan Babic of his duties as president of the Republic and not to give a vote of confidence to the entire government of Krajina, and this took place when the government of Krajina refused to adopt Vance's plan. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first Assembly to discuss this issue, the government positions with respect to Vance's plan was held on the 8th of December, 1991. It was the Assembly of the SAO Krajina and in Glina, under the presidency chairmanship of Milan Paspalj, part of the assembly met, part of the Assembly of the RSK met on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But as it says here, that the meeting was attended by 85 deputies of which 74 were in favour of the decision, 8 against, and 3 deputies refrained from voting. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were different reports as to the number of deputies who attended and how the voting went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's not true what this -- what it says in this report; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were different -- there was different information as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it goes on to say that at 1855 hours, over Serb radio in Knin, because it says at 1830 hours the meeting was concluded, so 15 minutes later there was an announcement broadcast over the Serb radio station of Knin and a telephone conversation was conducted with Dr. Milan Babic, in which he states that the meeting in Glina was unlawful and that it was held on the basis of instructions received from Belgrade. Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard that on the 9th of February, when Kostic, Hadzic were there, and it was proposed that Babic be replaced. And then Branko Kostic said, "Wait for us to leave."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what that means. I don't know what that means, that they should wait until they leave. I don't suppose they wanted to meddle in your internal affairs. That must be it. But anyway, tell me this: Is this part of the report in keeping with the facts? Because it states afterwards: "Milan Babic endeavours at all costs to retain power in Krajina. When he saw that he would not gain the support of the Assembly, he took a summary decision to set up new municipalities in those villages in which he has loyal representatives. Especially evident is the fact that some large places in the RSK which, until the reorganisation of the municipalities in the 1960s, were municipal seats, headquarters of the UDBA, the internal -- the UDBA in Kistanje did not receive these municipalities, although most of those places have more inhabitants than there are in the newly established municipal communities. And to convene the Assembly, he relates to Article 87 of the Constitution of the RSK, by which the president has the right to convene an assembly." Was that how it was or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what happened, according to the best of my recollections: It was an assertion of what was called the pink zones, or rather, that was a way for areas which were not incorporated by the Vance Plan to be represented in the political structures and for their stands and positions to be heard. So that was the basic political reason for which the municipalities were established in the area of Velika, Petrovo Polje, towards Drnis and at Skradin, and Vrhovine, et cetera. That's how they came into being. It is true that there were discussions about the formation, possible formation, once again, of the Udbina municipality. As far as I know, Babic did endeavour to remain in the realm of politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. However, it further states here that cadres policy, which was waged according to the system of placing his loyal men in each of these seats, this is boom ranging back on him, and the best example of this is the example of Mile Paspalj, who, as president of the Assembly after Babic's replacement, and Velibor Matijasevic, came back from anonymity, because Babic thought that everybody would be the subject of his manipulations, but this proved to be incorrect. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mile Paspalj came to the post of the president of the Assembly of the SAO, being proposed by the regional board of the SDS for Banija and Kordun. Mile Paspalj was the president of the regional board of the Serbian Democratic Party for Banija and Kordun and it was from that post that he took up the position of the president of the assembly of SAO Krajina on the 21st of November 1991. And on the 2nd of February, 1992, with Budimir Kosutic - that was my information anyway - he was under the influence, or rather, my information informed me that he went to Milosevic to change the -- his opinions of the Vance Plan. Because on the 31st of January, at an expanded session of the meeting, and on the 1st of February, he advocated the opinion of the government and of the Assembly of the SAO Krajina, and then on the 2nd of February he changed his opinion. And my information was that this was under the influence of Budimir Kosutic, and my information was that he had a secret meeting with Milosevic to discuss the issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is what it says further on in the report correct. It says: "Milan Martic, through his actions, showed that he remained loyal to the principles with which he set out at the beginning of the Knin events in August 1990, in the interests of the people that he wanted to see the Blue Helmets arrive as soon as possible and for peace to be restored. Therefore, Martic supported the urgent arrival of the United Nations mission and the deployment of the Blue Helmets, or rather, the creation of conditions to bring peace back to the area." Is that correct or not? Please give me a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Martic supported the policies of Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. He supported the policy of having the Vance Plan accepted and the Blue Helmets arrive and peace be established. That's right, isn't it? Now tell me this: Is it true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic, in December, or rather, January, the beginning of January, Martic was opposed to the application of the unconditional implementation of Vance's plan, and he advocated the positions of the government of the SAO and the Republic of Srpska Krajina for the plan to be modified. Later on he too accepted as Slobodan Milosevic's endeavours to apply the plan in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Krajina unconditionally as Slobodan Milosevic had agreed to in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you remember your own statement, what you said on the 18th of January, 1992 for Finnish television?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you is as follows: Is it true, as we're in private session - that you endeavoured that by refusing Vance's plan to represent yourself as a victim of some kind, a victim of the regime, and that you believed that you would be able to mobilise popular opinion in Serbia to your own ends, with the assistance of various opposition parties and thereby to destabilise the victims in that position and the relationship towards the problems of Krajina on the part of the authorities in Belgrade? Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I was a victim of your dictatorship, that is correct. However, in that context, the context you're talking about, linked to Vance's plan, the priority was security, the security and the future of the people living in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You wrote that famous letter that does not speak about security but speaks about all kinds of political -- very serious political qualifications, criticising me for the fact that I advocated the adoption of the Vance Plan, and I think that you remember that very well. So the weight of that letter did not lie in its security aspect and component but in its political sense; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter was designed to emphasise our positions, first and foremost, with respect to the engagement and involvement of the UN forces. That was our priority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I don't want to quote your own letter back to you again. But take a look at it. You said that Boro Rasuo in fact wrote the letter for you, or rather, a draft --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have the letter. My recollection is 92, but I could be wrong about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It should be 79, tab 79 of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 79. Yes. Let the witness have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be of assistance. They are newspaper articles, and in tab 9 of the letters, or rather, tab 80 contains the letters. And these are excerpts from newspaper articles in which those letters were published, whereas tab 80 contains both these two letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let him have 80 too. The point that was made to you, Mr. Witness, was that the letter - and we're looking at tab 80 - that you wrote did not contain an emphasis on security. Perhaps you'd like to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 3 of this letter that I signed says: "I want to use this imposed opportunity merely to clarify of use to you and the world public and at the same time disprove your arbitrary allegation that I am against peace, that I am in favour of war, and that my position stems from my alleged love of power and desire for political prestige." And then I go on to elaborate on the version of the Cyrus plan, Cyrus Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you can help us: Where do you deal with the question of security there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's reference to the term of six months, and we ask that this period be extended. That is at the end of the fourth paragraph. For any continuation of the use after six months, a new decision by the Security Council is necessary, together, of course, with the approval of the all parties in the conflict. In this specific case, this also includes Croatia. So that is an expression of our fear that after six months the mandate of the peace forces would not be extended, and as a result our security would be called into question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any other reference to the security aspect on this five-page letter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I go on to explain our positions regarding the confrontation lines, then again about the duration of the UN mandate, then also the possibility, if security were to be in jeopardy and the JNA would get involved, that that would be qualified as aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm afraid you won't find it. You can read it again, you can read the whole text once again. This letter was intended to discredit the authorities in Belgrade, or rather, me personally. And you were conducting a major campaign. Let me take you back to this interview with the Finnish television. Gentlemen, in English, it is RO 30-4565. It is dated the 18th of January, Belgrade. "Dr. Milan Babic, president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina [In English] having had a meeting with Serbian president Slobodan Milosevic, explaining Babic said that the letter has frozen his relations with us because he thinks that we have a duty to carry out resolutions that he adopts and imposes. Babic added that he did not seek contacts with Milosevic and that he expects Milosevic to apologise for the way he treated me, as a Serb and as a president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It is up to him to respond first." [Interpretation] Let me leave out some parts. "He also voices his suspicion that the Serbian president has entered [In English] some agreements that are not in our favour." [Interpretation] Into some agreements that are not in our favour. [English] "Slobodan Milosevic appropriated the right to make decisions on behalf of the Serbs from Krajina and to sign agreement to their detriment. We therefore must state clearly that he had no such right," Babic specified. [Interpretation] I assume that you know that I had emphasised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not an exhibit yet. It's a document presented as a Rule 68 material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that Cyrus Vance insisted that Serbia agree with this plan and that he did not believe that Serbia was deciding on your behalf but was agreeing in its own name with this plan of his and was putting its political influence behind it, the influence that it had over the citizens of the Republic of Serbian Krajina for the plan to be adopted? Were you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you respond, that -- since the interview was put to you, you can comment on that, if you disagree with anything that has been attributed to you. So perhaps you'd like to deal with that first, and then you can deal with the point which is made about Serbia having to agree. So is there anything you'd like to say about the interview, or do you agree that that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number of assertions were made. I gave a number of interviews, and as far as I can recollect, this could be and is in harmony with what I was saying in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Just a moment. Let the witness deal with the next point which you made about Cyrus Vance's insistence that Serbia agree. Now, you were asked whether you were aware of that or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We knew that Milosevic, Tudjman, and Kadijevic had adopted the plan and that we were being forced by Milosevic to accept the plan in the version in which they had accepted it. I remember that about a month or a month and a half of discussions over the plan, Mr. Cyrus Vance declared in New York, over the media, that Babic was Milosevic's problem, which meant that Milosevic should deal with the problem with Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to that statement, that Babic is Milosevic's problem, I think Cyrus Vance was right. Babic was a problem for all the people of Republic of Srpska Krajina and for Serbia, and that by his extremism, he caused a lot of trouble. I assume you will not deny that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Babic came to the official posts he held by legal means. At the elections, he was elected to those positions, and he performed a public office on the basis of a legal procedure whereby he had been appointed to it. So he enjoyed public support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish, since what is being put is a serious allegation. What's said is that the witness was a problem for all the people of the Republic of Serb Krajina and for Serbia, by his extremism, caused a lot of trouble. Now, Witness, what is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I think that I was not an extremist but was simply performing my public duties, which implied reflecting public opinion and expressing that public opinion on which my political office depended. I took over that office through the election procedure, after legal elections. As regards my positions regarding the Vance Plan, I won the support of the government and the Assembly of SAO Krajina, and a part of the Assembly of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, and after a three-day session in Belgrade, I was also given the support of the citizens of Knin, 10.000 inhabitants of Knin, who supported my decisions. On the 3rd of February, 1992, there were 5.000 people. I wanted to check Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. out the positions I advocated through the referendum for the public to say whether they agreed with those positions or not. The referendum was not carried out because it was prevented by people over which Milosevic had influence in Krajina. At the elections in 1993, as a presidential candidate, in the first round, according to all reports, or rather, the results of the first round, I got over half of the votes, more than all the other candidates put together. And then the elections were repeated several times. They were delayed unlawfully, so that Milan Martic, Milosevic's favourite, could win the elections. I believe that I did get support of the public opinion and the voters in Krajina for my positions, and I do not think that these were extremist positions. But from -- in retrospect, I think it was ethnoegoistic and that is why I look upon the period differently today, and with my present-day wisdom and from this distance, I would certainly not advocate the policy that you drew us into and that is a policy of national divisions, separatism, rifts, and interethnic conflicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I drew you all into that during my holidays in Kupari, when all this was going on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we're going to get much further with an exchange of that sort. No need to reply. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it clear to you that, apart from the fact that Serbia had to accept and support the Vance Plan, that the Vance Plan could not possibly be implemented without your agreement? Isn't that right? Were you aware of that, that it couldn't be implemented and that it would not be approved by the Security Council unless you also gave your approval?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why we made our objections. We were the party that was invited to state our views on the plan, and that is why we voiced our objections and took part in the discussions with the international mediators, and there were chances of the plan being partially modified, and it was partially modified, because we were asked to state our views about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can we then make it clear and agree that that plan could not be implemented without your approval and that your allegation that I had usurped the right to decide on your behalf is simply not right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not decide on your behalf. I could only decide to support the plan and to use my political influence towards you for you to support it as well. You decided in your own name, because you were a party to the conflict. You held the army in territory that should have been demilitarised, and that, I think, was the main reason. And the second was that you wanted to force us to agree with it too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. MILAN BABIC, Serbia was in the a party to the conflict in Croatia. Croatia was in conflict with the JNA and not with Serbia. Serbia was never a party to the conflict in Croatia. But we'll come to that a little later. So have we cleared up this point, that it was up to you and that you were fully aware at the time too that you had to decide about it, and that it was only our political influence that suggested you accept that plan? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had to also state our positions about it, us as well. That is why we were invited. But you were the one who agreed with it at the very outset.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not denying that I supported the Vance Plan and that I did everything I could to bring my influence to bear over you for you to accept it too. I'm not denying that. But as you yourself said that you took part in all this, look at this interview of yours, another one, that was as you were waging a full-fledged campaign at the time. So this is RO 304566, Belgrade, the 20th of January. The heading is: "The UN mission is condemned to failure." "'Without our consent,' [In English] says Milan Babic, president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, [Interpretation] in an interview published in today's edition of Borba. Borba was a leading federal newspaper in Yugoslavia in those days. 'It is certain that the UN Security Council and, above all, the Secretary-General will not set a precedent by sending in his forces to our territory and disarming the armed forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina without obtaining our consent,' Babic says." So, you see, it was clear to you that without your approval, this could not be. And surely that is why the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and not any people from Belgrade, decided, as it says in this report and as it has been recorded everywhere, that it decided, on the 16th of February, to accept the Vance Plan, and that the acceptance of that plan was carried out by the competent organ in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After your campaign and pressure, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my campaign was a political one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness must have a chance to deal with these matters. If you're going to put interviews to him, he should have a chance to deal with them and then deal with any subsidiary questions. You heard what it's alleged was said in the interview. Do you accept that that's correct or not? That's the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally was aware that we too had been invited to give our approval to the plan, namely, as the Presidency, the Rump Presidency of SFRY and Slobodan Milosevic were competent, or rather, the command of the armed formations in Krajina were under the command of the JNA, and through those forces they were also in command of the Territorial Defence, and through that they had control over the police in Krajina as well. So the point was that should the JNA withdraw from Krajina, the armed Territorial Defence would remain, and Milosevic would no longer have a command position through the JNA, via the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I really don't understand what that has to do, these nebulous explanations, which mean nothing, what that has to do with what I've just quoted. So please, let's be more specific. What does it go on to say in this interview. [In English] "We find the concept of involving UN peace forces unacceptable, according to which the territory of Krajina and Eastern and Western Slavonia are to be under UN protection as Croatian areas. The way Tudjman, Kadijevic, and Milosevic arrived at an agreement amounts to imposing a certain political solution that resembles or is identical to The Hague conference proposal about our special status within Croatia, Babic added." [Interpretation] Therefore, you were shooting from all weapons. I'm now speaking figuratively, referring to your politics. It was against the interests of Krajina. And here you explain indirectly why you rejected the special status that was offered you at the international conference and why you were waging a campaign in Knin against the authorities in Serbia, headed by me, saying that we were pushing you into this special status. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two things here. The first thing is that the essence of the plan was to demilitarise the area, and it was treated as different districts within Croatia. Secondly, the Croatian government and President Tudjman had already announced that with the arrival of the UN force they would establish their authority and had already appointed commissioners for each area in Krajina. So this was in this context that I gave these statements. The consequence of these statements was that the General Secretary of the United Nations acknowledged my objections and remarks, and in his reports that was adopted by the Security Council said that Croatian law would not apply in these territories, but rather, the legislation currently in force would continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those who were drafting this plan were well aware that it was not adopted as it was agreed. But answer this: You personally were given the explanation that the term is defined according to the usual rules of the Security Council, to be extended as required until the issue is resolved. So the term for which the UN forces are deployed, as I explained to you a number of times, believing, of course, the words of Cyrus Vance, who spoke the truth, that it would be extended as long as necessary.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two things here again. First, in the initial stage, in initial negotiations it was agreed that it would be six months, a term to be extended. However, we expressed our misgivings, saying that it's a short term, and eventually UN forces were deployed for an initial period of one year. Second, when references began to be made, when talks began about the Vance Plan, the international community had not recognised Croatia by that time. In the month of January, already a great number of countries, and on the 15th of January, all countries of Europe, and after that the United States, recognised Croatia as an independent state, and our fear that Croatia, as a future member of the United Nations, could obstruct the extension of the UN force mandate before the political solution for this area is found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt for a moment. Mr. Milosevic, you referred to two documents: One the interview with Finnish television on the 18th of January; second, the interview with Borba on the 20th of January. Do you want those documents exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us do that now. There are translations available, and perhaps the registry would give them numbers, please. Separate numbers, I think. Just a moment. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just wait for that to be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document dated January 18th will be D60, and the document dated January 20th will be D61.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, I'm using only the papers that I have received from you. Generally speaking, those interviews and verbal attacks were showered on me, in all the press, in all the media. But let us see what it says in this interview a little down below. [In English] Latest development in relations between the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Serbia, Babic pointed out the fact that there is dissatisfaction and disappointment among a large number of people who think that the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Serbian people have been abandoned by Serbia and the Serbian people in Serbia. It seems to me that the Serbian people's sentiments in Serbia do not correspond with Slobodan Milosevic's letter, Babic said."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thus, you were trying, in a way, to turn the public opinion, on the basis of people's feeling of solidarity, to manipulate public opinion in order to destabilise authorities in Serbia; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is a fact that you were turning your back on us. It is a fact - at least I saw it that way - that until then, you had been doing everything to keep everything under control, to wage the war, to keep us within Yugoslavia. You stirred up hatred between the Serb and the Croatian peoples. And then you were trying to pull out of this and abandon us. As for the political discussions and the vocabulary used, they were as they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was not disputable that I insisted that you go to Paris and other places to negotiate for peace. It wasn't disputed that I suggested you accept the decisions of The Hague conference. It was not disputed that I ultimately succeeded in getting the Assembly of Krajina to accept the Vance Plan. And still, I am the one who instigated you and stirred up hatred between Serbs and Croats, I, from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You waged the war and you created this hatred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to those facts some time later. Tell me this, coming back to the Finnish interview, where you say: "Deceiving the public [In English] there are no disagreements in the government of Krajina, and while answering the question of the support for Milosevic in Krajina, he said that it was negligible..." [Interpretation] Thus, you were trying to persuade the public that you will by all means succeed in rejecting the peace plan. These are only two interviews that you gave at that time. And you keep on asserting that the letter was written by Rasuo, did Rasuo also write these interviews and statements for TV and the press?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do they differ from this letter which, when you were quoting it some time ago, taking out only one neutral passage, you said: "I wrote it myself." Why are you trying to put a distance between you and the letter, to disassociate yourself from it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not trying to disassociate myself from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, I don't know if it is still necessary to continue in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from these events, let us come back to Jovan Raskovic, president of the SDS and founder of the Serb Democratic Party. I suppose you are not going to dispute that Professor Raskovic was a well-known, renowned psychiatrist; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was. He was a well-known doctor, academician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And even his research and work as psychiatrist elevated him to the position of member of the academy of sciences, and he was one of the most renowned psychiatrists in our country, well known throughout the world; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it disputed that Professor Jovan Raskovic, in addition to being an honourable man who was trying to resolve everything by peaceful means, was a very well-known, very competent, and very famous psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was well respected as a doctor and academician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. And is it true that on several occasions he emphasised having noticed in you a schizophrenic, narcissistic tendency? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not a proper question, any way, shape, or form. It's merely a comment, and sounds like a pretty cheap one at that. Yes. Next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is a very appropriate question, in the light of the issues we have been discussing in private session, because only a personality characterised by these features --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You're not a psychiatrist. You're supposed to be asking questions. I doubt whether that's -- you could call evidence about it. I doubt it very much, and it's not a proper question, from you or probably anybody else. And as I say, it sounds more like a cheap jibe. Now, you ask some proper questions of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, let me be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that these characteristics of yours have some influence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is not a proper question. I've just ruled on it. Now, move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suppose that you will not allow this. Could we perhaps in this connection just hear a comment from that intercept? I will remind you, because I don't want to look for it now in this heap, the one where the witness is not going to a meeting, a very important meeting for the interests of the people he was representing, only because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he's refusing to go abroad to attend a meeting because he is not being treated with enough respect as head of the government, president of the Republic, or whatever he was at the time, and that it is not only a display of vanity, but a complete lack of responsibility towards the people he was representing, because this was a peace conference. And you had been quoting this intercept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the question is whether this was a matter of prestige and treatment that was more important to you than the need for peace negotiations, that it was a matter of prestige and whether you would be treated with the proper respect for head of government or head of state. That was more important to you than the need to make peace?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you answer, we'll get a reference for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's tab 15 of the intercept binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, if you'd like to answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation was as follows: My political stance was that the SAO Krajina should be represented on an equal footing as a party involved in the peace conference, and not participate just in the committee for national minorities. So it was not about personal prestige.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is this claim made by people who then occupied leading positions correct? After the conference in The Hague, he convened a session of the government of Krajina, and most of the people were leaders from Knin. So you convened a session of the government in Krajina, you were furious with me, and you told them, your colleagues in the government of Krajina, that I was forcing you to accept the special status. You told them that all I wanted was to get rid of you and to leave you in Croatia, which you would never accept. Is this claim of your colleagues and members of the leadership and government of Krajina at that time correct? Was it indeed the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you had two different approaches to me and to the representation of our political position at The Hague conference. One was displayed on the 20th of October, when you were forcing us to accept The Hague documents, and later your position changed; it was a bit different. Those four items that you proposed did not fit in well with The Hague documents, the ones that were envisaged for discussion for my third meeting with Wijnaendts. I don't know which one you are referring to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've got past the time for a break, so we should adjourn. You can return to this afterwards. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're resuming in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To avoid confusion, the two points around Carrington's plan, the second was my public speech at The Hague conference, when I stood up in opposition to the attempt to have Yugoslavia, and that's what I said on the occasion, be abolished with a stroke of the pen. So I was opposed to the abolition of Yugoslavia, and that has nothing to do with what I've just asked you, which relates to the question of Krajina and special status for it. So your associates say that he was angry at me, furious at me, that I was forcing him to accept this special status and that I said that I just wanted to get rid of you and to leave you in Croatia, which would never be accepted; is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the 20th of October, you prevailed upon us to accept special status, according to documents of The Hague conference, as stipulated there, and on the 23rd of October, you told me that we should accept special status on Yugoslav soil.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not correct. But never mind. Let's continue with what I was saying. Your associates at that time, the people around you, said we know that none of us commented on that because we had respect towards me and considered that that was probably a good thing when it came to special status. Therefore, that Babic, on his own, in the name of that government, made the decision to reject the special status. Is that how it was or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was. I always consulted the government, or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rather, I presented my views to it. And what happened was that I did not reject the special status but it was always noted that we would continue negotiations on that issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm asking you now about what people claimed, and they're ready to testify here to that effect, and they say the following: "On his own initiative, on behalf of the government, that never met, he proclaimed himself member of the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina and Milan Martic, without his knowledge, appointed him deputy commander." Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we have here a decision signed by you appointing Milan Martic deputy commander of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the basis of authorisation from the Prime Minister, pursuant to the law on National Defence of the Republic of Serbia which the government of SAO Krajina, on the 1st of August, 1991, made a decision to apply as a law which was in force on the territory of the SAO Krajina, and of course he agreed with that, with that appointment, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that in the autumn of 1991 you forced the command of the TO for Lika, Colonel Pero Trbojevic, to effect mobilisation over night in the Gradacac municipality and Donji Lapac municipality, in the Municipal Assemblies there, and to expel all the Croats, armed and unarmed, from Gracac, towards Gospic, or rather, Medak. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've already spoken about that. I said and explained how Colonel Trbojevic arrived -- went to Colonel Vukovic and asked him to assist mobilisation of the 1st Light Brigade or the 1st Territorial TO Brigade, as it was referred to. So what is true is that I launched an appeal for people to respond to mobilisation for that particular brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they say differently. They say that the JNA's intention was to free the Sveti Rok warehouse at Medak, which was a military facility, a military storehouse near Medak, but that the plan almost fell through because of your -- the fact that you were in a hurry, you personally, because people moved towards Gospic who were not trained properly. And what happened was that the Croatian policemen fled and then you yourself, together with your volunteers, most of them criminals, set fire to those villagers and Lovrinac was the largest of them. Is that what happened, and that's how you took Sveti Rok too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you ascribed this as being a success of yours. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And is the following correct, what was also claimed: That in order to play up to the Chetnik organisation in Chicago and the Vojvoda Chetnik leader Momcilo Djujic, whom you expected to get money from in 1991, you played up to them and you personally brought in a law to ban the work of the Communist Party.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th of January, 1992, a decree was passed which I myself signed in the capacity of President of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, to ban communist parties, organisations, movements, on the territory of Srpska Krajina, not in order to play up to Momcilo Djujic, but because this was a political assessment. We thought this was a way to distance ourselves from you and your policies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you did distance yourself from Serbia all the time and did what you did. So this is in contradiction, considerable contradiction with what happened to your distancing from the Republic of Serbia and for what you claim happened following orders and instructions from Serbia. However, now you said it wasn't a law but a decree.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a decree that was passed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. You're quite right. I have here, pursuant to Article 78, "the President of the RSK enacts a law to ban the work," et cetera, et cetera, "and functioning of all communist parties, organisations and meetings on the territory." And then it goes on to say: "Their work is banned and political activities banned, and Article 2 of the law comes into force immediately." So that has only two articles. So you personally passed a law and you even took over powers of legislation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of a general article of the Constitution of the RSK, it was interpreted by experts that by following this article and by relying on that article, invoking it - it was of a political nature - we could pass such a decree. It had no legal form. It was, rather, a political one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that in order to rid yourself of Jovo Raskovic, you proclaimed professor Raskovic to be a traitor who collaborating with Tudjman for the sole purpose -- only because he negotiated and talked with Tudjman about a peaceful solution, just for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. While Professor Raskovic was negotiating with Tudjman, I was on very good terms with him, and I said that a faction did indeed exist which was opposed to this, and entered into polemics with Professor Raskovic. The first polemics I had with Professor Raskovic was around the 17th of February, 1991, with respect to the way in which the Serbian Democratic Party was being organised, or rather, this was a polemics to do with changes in the statute of the SDS and with respect to the constitution of regional boards. Up until that time, I don't recall having any public polemics with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you say you didn't lead a campaign, wage a campaign, of compromising Professor Raskovic for the meetings he had with President Tudjman; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people who made statements with respect to that. I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Why, then, for what happened in Dubica are you accusing Milan Martic, are you holding him responsible for the Dubica events, when you know full well that the perpetrators were criminals from the SDS, as it says here in the claims made by your then associates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who carried that out. I said what I knew about the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that at that time Milan Martic did not even take -- had not taken control of those areas yet and that your main man, the principal man for Dubica in the SDS at that time was Kostar [phoen], Mile Misljenovic, Kostar. Is that right or not. He was a postman, Mile Misljenovic, the postman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What event are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About the events in Dubica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said exactly what I knew about those events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say so, judging by what they claim here. And is it true that before the conflict in Kijevo near Knin you exerted pressure constantly on the command of the corps, that is to say General Spiro Ninkovic, Ratko Mladic, and that it was your village, your native village of Kukor at Vrljika that was blocked and that an attack had to be launched in order to free that area? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to you about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- when I asked why that attack -- that they told me, their answer was to me that they had to liberate Kumrovec.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke about the events around Vrljika and Kutusa [phoen]. You said: "Hasn't that been settled already?" And I learnt later on on that particular morning there was indeed an attack on Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that you learnt what happened, although you were actually there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with you on the 26th, one day before, rather, on the very day the attack took place. I arrived in the evening of the previous day. I arrived in Belgrade. I was told to go and see you, and I went to your offices on two occasions and we talked about Frenki, Spiro Nikolic, and about the problems related to Vrljika, and then I left. And you commented on that, and you said, "Hasn't that been settled already?" Just as what you said about Frenki, that he should be in Krajina because he's a good man. And you asked about Spiro Nikolic, what kind of commander he was, and I said, "Well, his conduct is proper." I had nothing for or against him. So that was on that particular day, when the JNA, with all its units under its command, attacked Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that in that attack on Kijevo, there were no fatalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't know the number the people who were killed or wounded or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it says here that there were no casualties at Kijevo and the Croatian police had previously killed a young man from the village of Polace, whose name was Vaso Pecer, several days before the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vaso Pecer died around the 2nd of May, 1991, in some incidents that took place there and which were caused by a DB group and police from Golubic, which means at the random shooting at Kijevo, in May 1991, and the JNA attacked Kijevo on the 26th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, is it possible -- may I read out, in an open session, a denial which was sent in by Marko Dobrijevic, secretary of the Serbian Democratic Party and director of the communal enterprise in Knin during the war and a deputy of the last Assembly, when it convened, the Assembly of Serbian Krajina, which he signed. The denial is signed by him, and underneath he says that he agrees that this statement be made public here in the trial against me. He makes mention of MILAN BABIC. He doesn't mention his name anywhere in text. But I should nonetheless like to ask, and I do believe that it is your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wish too, that the proceedings here are public. So I would like to read this out in public, in open session, if I may, so that we may comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can put to the witness what has been given to you in that statement. You can't exhibit it, for the reasons you know about. You must let the witness have the opportunity to respond to the various allegations that are made, no doubt, in it. As for whether it should be in open session, provided it doesn't identify the witness, then it can be in open session. But if at any stage it does, then we must go into private session to do it. But you can begin in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have here a statement with respect to the testimony of witness MILAN BABIC, and the statement was sent by Marko Dobrijevic, secretary of the SDS and director of the communal enterprise in Knin during the war and a deputy of the last Assembly of Serbian Krajina. And along with his acquiescence, he has signed the document with his name and surname. He signed it in full and he would like me to make it public. It says here as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Listen, whatever he wants, whether he wants it made public or not, it doesn't matter. All that's relevant is that you can put to the witness something which you say contradicts him. Now, it's his evidence which matters, not what's in the document. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, I think that it is in the interests of the truth that this statement be read out, and the witness will answer my questions once I have read out the statement, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You're not going to read the statement out, because it's not evidence. But what you can put is sections of the statement to the witness for his comment. He must be allowed to comment as you go through. You can't simply read the statement out as though it was evidence. Yes. Now, put what's in the statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in the statement, it states that everything that the witness did was wrong and that now in The Hague he is accusing others. He claims that he never even met some individuals and that he's either putting them in one bag of tricks that existed only in his mind. And this is what he mentions. You mentioned Jovica Stanisic, for whom you've heard only on television. Do you know that Jovica Stanisic has married, from Javrsak, near Knin, and that he's with his in-laws, or he went to visit his in-laws before the war and during the war. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Jovica Stanisic on many occasions, at your office for the first time, in 1990; in January 1991 as well; I also saw him in your offices in March 1991; I saw him in his own office in March 1991, and February too; and I think I saw him on quite a number of other occasions as well. And I said that here in Court, that Jovica Stanisic is married to a woman from Javrsak, he told me that in the Seher restaurant in August 1991 when he introduced me to his wife and when he said that Captain Dragan owed them some money which they had paid out for some DB services, and he went off with that money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he came to his in-laws, to visit them before the war and during the war; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says here in your sick imagination, everyone who came from Serbia came there because they were sent by the DB of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's simply an allegation. You needn't bother to answer that. Yes. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says as follows: All the structures, Mr. MILAN BABIC, all the structures that you call parallel structures were created precisely by you: The staff in Golubic was created by you. Without anyone's knowledge, on your own initiative you proclaimed a state of war on the 17th of August, 1990. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The staff in Golubic, which functioned for a certain period of time at the end of August until the beginning of September, in 1990? Golubic was formed at a session of the Serbian Democratic Party chaired by Dr. Jovan Raskovic on the 18th of August, 1991. That session was held in Padjene, and the initiator for forming that staff was Maruo Dobrijevic, Jovan Opacic, Dusan Zelenbaba, Branko Peric, and Milan Martic. The state of war was proclaimed in Knin in 1990, in August 1990, as I have already testified here in this court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true what he says, that you were seriously criticised by the Federation to conceal your responsibility, you shifted the blame on Snezana Stamatovic, a journalist in Radio Knin? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't mention that lady.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are going now in a lot of details and I think we should be in private session for all these details.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there's no need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we are going to approach anything which may identify the witness, we should go into private session. But we'll go on for the moment in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says that you were lying by accusing Serbia and the leadership of Serbia for the creation of parallel authorities in Krajina, whereas all the appointments were done personally by you and, unfortunately, arbitrarily. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding parallel structures in Krajina, what their function was and who did it, I've already testified about that here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I was able to notice when I asked you to list at least a few names from Serbia, you managed to name four people, some of whom could not have been there because they were working in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been over that. We've no need to go over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The parts that may be identifying, we'll avoid reading, not to prompt the other party to ask for a closed session. So I'll refer to that later on in private session. He goes on to say here: "You are claiming that Croats were expelled from Knin, and you know very well that those are lies. The truth is that those people who had responded to Tudjman's invitation to leave Krajina were leaving. My driver was Andrija Butkovic from Knin, who was employed in 1993 when the war was in full swing and he was a Croat. Bosiljka Curko, working in the public utility company in Knin, when she was leaving Knin, at Tudjman's invitation, I personally appealed to her to stay and said if she was afraid, her whole family could stay with my family. And she said that was not the point. 'Others are leaving, so I'm leaving too.' She bid farewell to everyone and brought me a bottle of whiskey and of course we embraced upon parting. Throughout the war, up to 1995, the main water tank was guarded by a Croat, Stipe Gambiroza. Also a Croat delivered food to the kindergarten in Knin throughout the war. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have testified to the best of my knowledge about those events here in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. At a competition for the best balcony in Knin, three awards were distributed, 300, 200, and 100.000. The first two prizes were won by Croatian women and a third by a Serbian woman. And all this was announced on Radio Knin. What kind of expulsion are you talking about? So I'm asking you the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the best balcony competition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was it right that there were some Croats who remained in Knin, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were. I know them. There was my neighbour, Grandmother Kaja. Let me mention her. There were others too. I don't want to mention names. I spoke of the serious suffering of Croats in Kijevo, when the JNA attacked the village with artillery. I spoke about the terrible, awful expulsion of Croats from Vrpolje in 1993. I spoke about the fact that the Croats in Knin did not feel at ease in an atmosphere of interethnic and political conflict. And I also mentioned the events from April 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to go over those events again. It's just that question of whether some remained. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's very, very good, because the next quotation from this statement denies precisely what you are saying. He says: "If that had been so, would the Knin Croats, in 1996, that is, after Storm, would they have signed a petition calling on the Serbs to return to Knin? Unfortunately, Mr. Curko, who handed the petition to the Sabor in Zagreb was met and beaten up by HDZ members." Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of the details, but I do know that many Croats from Knin were sorry that the Serbs had left Knin and that they did express their wish for them to return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go on. In a location Rupe, in which, according to the witness, Croatian civilians were killed, everyone knows that these are fabrications. Those civilians who remained ate together with the army members, the JNA. There's a case of Ivan Tepic, from Rupe, who asked to join his family in Sibenik, which of course he was allowed to do, but after arriving in Sibenik, he said how the Serbs hadn't hurt him but, on the contrary, they had given him food which they themselves were short of, and he was killed by Croats in Sibenik. I will not go on to read what relates to you in person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But regarding this particular event, I was talking about the trial to the -- of the perpetrators of crimes, and I recall that there was a trial of a group from Zelenik, for an event that took place -- Drvenik, I'm sorry. I think the reason was that one of their men was killed somewhere around Rupe and that they took revenge for this over their neighbour Croats. They killed them, and that is why they were put on trial. So I referred to this in that context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Probably you mixed something up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not quite sure whether the crime evented near Rupe or in Drvenik, Ervenik, and then I corrected myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't even remember where your testifying about what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember they committed a crime against their neighbours and that is why they were put on trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He asked: "Why he is not testifying about the 10.000 missing civilians that were withdrawing from the Croatian army together with American instructors who were sowing death on innocent, old men and women, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. some of whom did not wish and some of whom could not leave their homes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a question that the witness can deal with. That's a comment by whoever wrote the letter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Dobrijevic says that the SDS was formed near a pit in Lika, where, during the Second World War the Ustasha criminals, with the help of Hitler, were building the statehood of Croatia based on crimes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Totally irrelevant. Yes, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that where the SDS was formed, Mr. MILAN BABIC?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of January, 1990, Television Belgrade broadcast that Academician Raskovic had announced the formation of a Serb party in Croatia. Later on, from the participants in that meeting in Serb, I heard that there was a ritual performed over the pit, a religious ritual, at the pit Kuk, near Lapac, where the Ustashas in 1941, had killed and thrown the killed Serbs into that pit. A strange ritual took place to mark the beginning of the formation of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you comment on what Dobrijevic says? "As regards a witness hidden by a screen, I would just ask him where all those fabrications come from. He's testifying about areas on which he never set foot."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a worthless comment, completely worthless. Now, let's move on, and relevant questions. Your time is going, Mr. Milosevic. Unless you ask proper questions, it will come to an end. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case, I'll shorten this to a maximum degree. Dobrijevic says here, and there are many explanations here relevant to this witness -- he says: "I'm writing this on behalf of the slaughtered children of the Konevi [phoen] Bridge on behalf of those in Jasenovac --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. These are totally improper questions. Whatever he thinks he's doing, it is of no relevance to this Trial Chamber. Now, if there's anything -- you can put anything which is relevant, which contradicts the witness's testimony. What you can't put is abuse from the writer of the letter. It doesn't matter at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is not someone. It is one of the closest associates. It is just not anyone, but one of the closest associates of this witness, who has carried out this about-turn, for the reasons that are well known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can call the witness in due course. Meanwhile, all you can do is to put anything relevant to him which contradicts his evidence. But facts only, not abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think it is not abuse if we're establishing untruths. But as we're in open session, I will not go into any details that identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question, therefore, would be, on the basis of what we've been saying here over the past several days and partially on the basis of what I've just read to you, and also on the basis of the explanations you yourself gave to the investigators, it follows that you had one thing on your mind, you did another, and spoke a third, whereas in fact, as you yourself are saying, you advocated peace and life within Croatia. Now, tell me, please: Did you say to me, or anyone in Serbia, what your peaceful efforts were? Because neither I nor anyone else could undermine your peace-seeking efforts when, to this day, neither I nor anyone else in Serbia, and to tell you the truth, in Krajina too, knew nothing about your peace efforts. So tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness MILAN BABIC, that was a lengthy comment or question. Perhaps we'll hear -- what is the question, put shortly, please, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell me, or anyone else in Serbia, or anyone in Krajina -- ever present an idea about any peace efforts of yours whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last one was on the 8th of August, 1995, the proposal, that is, my agreement with the Z-4 plan and the other elements of the conversation I had with Mr. Galbraith, and I asked for your support. Before that, I also spoke to you about the Z-4 plan. We also discussed with Borisav Jovic, in August 1990, questions of security and a political settlement for the crisis that was looming. And he supported our propositions on your behalf, because you were influencing him, and you told him to tell us that you would support our political struggle and that the JNA would protect that political struggle. You gave us instructions how to carry out the political referendum, on what legal basis. You said that a law was in preparation for the self-determination of nations, that that was a legal model, and this was a model that we supported. That was your model, and we supported that model, believing it to be a legal one that would bring peace to the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why are you involving the JNA, when there were no conflicts in 1990 and the role of the JNA in those days was not of current interest? Didn't you construe all that solely on the basis of the fact that you established that, by coincidence, there were several people on holiday at the same time? Isn't that evidence of your narcissism, if you're sending me a message for me to receive you and I tell you that someone in the SFRY Presidency should receive you, that you come to the conclusion that I have a military staff meeting to decide who would receive you; that whenever somebody announces that he wants to receive me, that I have to have a top-level conference to make a decision about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not making any constructions; I'm just conveying what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, according to that knowledge, for instance, Hamdija Podzerac was on a holiday at the same time, who was then a member of the Presidency from Bosnia-Herzegovina, a Muslim. Maybe I consulted him too whether I should receive Milan Babic or whether somebody from the Presidency should receive him, and another 3.000 or so other people holidaying there. Who knows how many of them could have been consulted as to whether Milan Babic should be received.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what I knew. We went to see you, not the others, not the other 3.000. You didn't come to see me. You went to see Jovic. Through Slobodan Bukatic [phoen], we contacted you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will have occasion to discuss that later. In this paper written by Dobrijevic, which I didn't want to read in open session, it says you personally amassed so many functions upon yourself that people called you "Little Tito," "Little Tito," alluding to our former president. I'm explaining in case you don't understand what it means in our language. And it says statistics experts from that time counted 32 positions that you held, the most important of them being president of the National Council, president of the Republic, head of government, president of the municipality, president of the Serb Democratic Party. Is it true that you held all these positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said in this courtroom about all the positions I held -- maybe not all. I don't know. At various times I held different posts. I was president of the municipality for about four years. I was president of the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. I was president of the National Council from the 31st of July, 1990 until the 28th of February of 1991, approximately, when this council ceased to exist. I was president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina from 19 December 1991 until the 16th February 1992. Was there any other position that you asked me about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, judging by all I know, these positions were held by you in succession, not at the same time. If you were four years president of the municipality of Knin, you were also president of the SDS simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was president of the Municipal Assembly of Knin for the longest time, and this position coincided with various other functions for a while. I was head of government from the 29th May 1991 until 19th December 1991, when this position was held by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Vice-president. He was acting in this position.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was president of the Municipal Assembly of Knin and president of the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party for the longest time.
