utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So head of government until end 1991, then you were president of the Republic, and then you became head of government again, president of the Serbian Democratic Party. A moment ago you were saying that you always followed legal procedure throughout your political career. Is it therefore indisputable that nobody appointed you to these positions from Serbia? Is that at least undisputed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was elected to my posts by citizens, public positions such as president of the municipality, president of the Executive Council, Prime Minister, president of the Republic. From this position, I was replaced through an intervention from Serbia. Then to my positions in the party I was elected by party organs. I was elected president of the National Council by the members of that council, headed by Jovan Raskovic, who was a member of that council.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Jovan Raskovic, president of that council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were elected by the electorate, and my pressure only caused you to be replaced from some positions. Or pressure from Belgrade. As you wish. And the reason was your rejection of the peace plans.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You used my rejection of the Vance Plan, as you had adopted it, to replace me from that position and put Mihajlo Markovic instead, in 1991. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. He said he used the Vance Plan to get rid of Babic, and then he suddenly realised what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Vance Plan was rejected and the intervention of the UN force was required to replace Babic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Markovic told me that about a year later. The conflict with you was used to replace me from my post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a matter of personal sympathy or antipathy, not any objective reasons, I suppose. Tell me now, since you were not afraid, you were not in the least frightened by all these radical acts that your associates are talking about, and even in your statement to the investigators you say that you had become an ethnoegotist, that you were overcome by vanity, that you neglected the suffering of others. We have this on tape. Tell me now: How could I, or anyone else, have influenced a man like you, a man overcome by vanity, fear, self-love, desire to please - these are all things you said yourself - rather than striving to resolve the problems of the people you represented?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for fear, I even said, in the beginning of March 1991, that Croats are threatening us, jeopardising us, and instilling fear. After the Spegelj affair, you frightened us with Ustashas, genocide, and you made me believe that self-determination of peoples after secession is a legal way out, a legal path. With your political position and the authority you held - and I believed you - convinced me that it is the right way to go. The right of peoples to self-determination is something I accepted from you, and thus entered this vicious circle, this condition of ethnocentrism, which I was unable to shed until 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you now questioning the right of peoples to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, Yugoslavia was made up of peoples who exercised their rights within republics as federal units of Yugoslavia and on the federal level in matters in which republics were supposed to agree on, such as the constitution of Yugoslavia. You explained, and you convinced us, that if somebody wishes to leave Yugoslavia, they have the right to. But administrative borders within Yugoslavia cannot be the borders defining this division. You said that the prevailing authoritative borders were the ones determined by referendums. Borisav Jovic explained that the smallest unit is a municipality, and he said that after a referendum on self-determination of people, the municipalities from a republic which opts for leaving Yugoslavia -- municipalities wishing to stay should remain within Yugoslavia. Borisav Jovic explained that it was your position. And it is precisely this option that led us to war and misfortune for all the peoples of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your opinion, it was not the violent secession of Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia that caused the war, it was the right of people to self-determination; is what you're claiming now? I have to ask you this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war was caused by your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time. Now, let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war was caused by your way. You caused the war, because you wanted, by violent means, through the JNA and other armed formations that you controlled, to take over parts of the territory of other republics which you believed should remain within the new state that you were in the process of establishing. The rationale and explanation for this that you put forward was the right of peoples to self-determination. However, you did not respect this right. You waged war even on those territories which were not majority-Serb territories and where people had not declared themselves in favour of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that these are questions of vital importance. They do not reveal the identity of the witness, and these things should, I believe, be heard in public session. All of these things that the witness is saying, in the opinion of the amici, are things that should be heard by the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The danger is that some form of his identity may be revealed. Mr. Milosevic, are you going to deal with matters now that will reveal the identity of the witness or can we go back into open session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the witness who opened the door to an issue which certainly requires a private session. He's putting things upside down here, and he's overestimating his intelligence and his knowledge, which again proves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us not go into it now. We'll remain in private session. Now, your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you feel repentance and shame for your part in all these events. You are saying things diametrically opposite to the things that you were telling us when we were discussing issues of peace and war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repent for having become an ethnoegoistic, for accepting your thesis that people of the former Yugoslavia should separate. That kept me convinced for a long time that all that Serbs were doing for self-determination was right. But you yourself soiled even your own thesis. I repent forever accepting that policy, for embracing it, for having liked it. That's true. I am sorry that I was an egotist at the time. I'm sorry because I am now fully convinced that it was the primary cause for all the things that eventually happened, and especially the way in which you did it. It was horrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I think this particular question could be asked in public session as well. I'll ask it and leave it to your judgement. Since it is not disputed that you repent, you hold yourself out to be a person who always advocated and worked for peace, why didn't you return to Knin? Because authorities there would meet you with understanding, in view of all your peace efforts. You say that peace was always on your mind, although it was not on your lips.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You convinced us that it was necessary to wage war with Croatia. The Croat people suffered, and since they could not take their revenge on you, they would take their revenge on someone else, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe this question could be asked in public session, Mr. May, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one I just asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I think not. Very well it revealed his identity. It was a personal question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. Let us move back into open session and refrain from personal questions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we note that you claim that the war in Yugoslavia was not caused by the violent secessions, first of Slovenia, then Croatia, and finally Bosnia and Herzegovina, not even the illegal secessions? It was caused, rather, by an interpretation of the right of peoples to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the war, the armed conflict in Slovenia, began when the Republic of Slovenia assumed control over border crossings --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us not talk about Slovenia. I'm just asking you: Was the war caused by the violent secessions of these republics or by the right of peoples to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war in Croatia was caused by you, by creating incidents, by involving the Yugoslav People's Army into the conflict, and by commanding the JNA against the Republic of Croatia and inflicting damage upon the Croatian people, as well as the Serbian people, whom you had pushed into war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is not going to identify you. You said a moment ago that this happened because of the right of peoples to self-determination. Tell me: Have you read the constitutions of Yugoslavia that existed throughout Yugoslavia's existence? Do you know that it says that the peoples of Yugoslavia had united to create Yugoslavia using their rights to self-determination, peoples, not republics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's what the constitution says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what does it mean, then, to invoke the right of peoples to self-determination, a right that every people in Yugoslavia shares? Why does it mean that this right caused the war rather than the violent secession of other republics who didn't wish to stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yugoslavia was made up of republics, as far as I understand, and I am not a lawyer competent or qualified to interpret the constitution. The constitution also said that peoples exercise their rights within republics, and on the Yugoslav federal level, they exercise it through republics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Since you really aren't an expert in constitutional matters, I don't wish to abuse your lack of knowledge, your ignorance on that score. But you said that it was my thesis to separate the peoples. Anybody who has read any one of my speeches would have concluded right the reverse. I said that I considered that Yugoslavia was the best possible solution for all the Yugoslav peoples, in which they lived together, freely and on a footing of equality. And I advocated the preservation of Yugoslavia. Isn't that true, Mr. MILAN BABIC?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You strove for the fact that the Serbs from Croatia and the Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina should enjoy the right to remain within Yugoslavia, that is to say, in the kind of Yugoslavia that you were reorganising. That was your public stance. What you in fact did was that in the areas inhabited by the Serbs, not only where they were the majority but where they were the minority as well, you caused incidents to take place and then deployed the Yugoslav People's Army in order to retain those territories by force of violence within that state, sidestepping the decisions of the majority in the territories where they were living, and by creating incidents and waging a war, you fanned the flames and you incited Slovenia and Croatia to step down from the state of Yugoslavia and the state that you were creating. That is how I understood your conceptions of the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, others didn't understand it in this way. Now, what your understanding was under the circumstances in which you find yourself today, I'm not wondering about that now. But let's be a little more specific with respect to your accusations and the fabrications and the fact that dangers were conjured up to which the Serb people were exposed to in Croatia. During your examination-in-chief here, you claimed, and I think that we even saw an excerpt played from the film, the tape, about Spegelj, this film of Spegelj was a fabrication. It was a forgery. And that the Federal Secretariat for National Defence played it. That was what was claimed, that it was played as a sort of propaganda device, in order to incite clashes and conflict. And that it was just propaganda, pure and simple. So please answer me this: Do you know what weapons, if it was indeed a forgery, what weapons were they using to shoot from at that same JNA in Croatia and at the Serbs in Croatia, and whether or not those soldiers and those compatriots of yours that were being killed from some Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sort of forged or falsified weapons as well that had been conjured up that you saw heard about in this falsified document and tape about Spegelj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said with respect to the Spegelj tape two facts: First I had heard that Spegelj himself had denied certain statements and observations made in the film; and second, I said, and I can repeat that if you like, that the film itself caused a frightening effect on the Serb people, especially the Serb people in Croatia and in Knin itself, because it was in that film and via that tape that it was stated that the Croatian government, the Croatian authorities, would slaughter the Serbs in Knin, that it would kill the officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, their wives, and that this would be a general slaughterhouse. And this caused great reaction and hostility towards the Croatian government. And the Croatian government, or rather, its special police force, and especially its guard corps, used real weapons against the armed formations and units of the Yugoslav People's Army and all the other units which were under its control and command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was, then, a propaganda campaign, was it, to frighten the Serbs? Or was it a taster of -- by the Federal Ministry of Defence of what was to come, the dangers in store, the dangers that threatened, because of illegal arming and the threats that were being made and the wave of nationalism that was rampant in Croatia and the violent secessions? Is that what you're claiming? That's what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information put out in this way resulted in the hostility of the Serb people towards the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In view of the fact that the other side has pulled out of context just one segment, a brief segment of that film, it was a brief excerpt, which wasn't live, but we had a still photograph of it, and just heard the voice. I'm now going to play that same tape which the other side tendered as a piece of evidence. It is a brief excerpt, once again. But other parts of that same tape. And they don't last more than two minutes altogether. So may we have a look at that tape? Let's look at that forgery, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When we have the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the Spegelj tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, tab 170 from Exhibit 352.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we'll have it played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] That same night in which the previous conversations took place, eight [Indiscernible] trucks intended for the terrorist army of the HDZ on the 20th of October crossed our borders.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters apologise, but they do not have the transcript of this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here you have the illegal introduction of weapons from Hungary. Look at Spegelj live and see what he says here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, but they're not able to follow. "SPEAKER: ...throughout the territory of 5th Military District Solvenia, the whole of Croatia and part of Bosnia, we now have armed 800.000 with Kalashnikovs. Let only 10.000 of them get arms. The army has nothing to look for there. We cut down. I have a problem now to protect you, the two of you, not from the army but from others. Fuck you. Each officer is covered by five in Virovitica and they will be cut down at their own homes. I have to give a list. You'll get it tomorrow. I have to quickly state now that this will be Virovitica. There's no question of that. Nobody must leave the barracks alive, nobody. I know that we -- I must now quickly inform those lads in Virovitica who to spare, who not, absolutely not. No one is to be allowed to reach the barracks, no one. One of the two men I know, for example, we make those --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were brief excerpts. This is the original tape that was filmed as it was explained by the Military Intelligence Service of the day. Spegelj, without a doubt, is the man talking, and he was brought to trial in Zagreb later on. You saw in the first portion there was the illegal introduction of weapons from Hungary, with all the lists and records and documents necessary. And in one of your -- I don't want to identify the conversation you had, because we'll have to go back into private session once again, but you claimed that I armed you with some sort of weapons from Hungary, and the whole of Yugoslavia knows very well who imported weapons from Hungary and who it was that armed themselves from Hungary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now: Did you ever receive any kind of weapons from Hungary whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the 20th of April, 1991, you said that you had purchased 20.000 pieces of weaponry in Hungary for us. This was a little strange and a little funny because the public was informed in this way that weapons were bought by the government of Croatia in Hungary, and later on I learnt that this was not so, that you had bought weapons in Hungary, but that you in fact distributed weapons from the warehouses of the Territorial Defence in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this would seem to me to be nonsense too, this matter of Serbia purchasing weapons in Hungary. And secondly, have you forgotten what you yourself said earlier on, that you procured weapons from the Territorial Defence warehouses in Krajina, and from the TO warehouses in Western Bosnia and you even mentioned the name of a lieutenant colonel who supplied you with the weapons, that the TO warehouse had somewhere around Bihac or wherever. Have you forgotten about all that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Serbs in Krajina were armed from two sources. One source was from Serbia, via the DB of Serbia, the state security of Serbia, and the second was by the JNA in the Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you claim that you never said that you got your weapons from the Territorial Defence warehouses in Krajina and in Bosnia; is that what you're saying? But that you were supplied exclusively from Serbia and by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Bosna and Krajina are concerned, I mentioned the Bihac airport, which is partially in Bosnia-Herzegovina and partially in Croatia, or rather, Krajina. Now, where the Bihac airport base is located in more specific terms, I said I don't know, but I said I know that weapons came in through two roads into Krajina, one from Serbia, the Grahovo direction, and the other was from Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you were not supplied from the Territorial Defence warehouse in Krajina, you were not supplied by -- from the Territorial Defence warehouse in the Bihac region, but you were supplied by Serbia and the JNA; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA supplied us with weapons, that is to say, in concrete terms, the Bihac area, Sveti Rok, and also in part the Knin Corps distributed weapons, I don't know where from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you organise demonstrations in front of the Knin Corps to call for weapons to be distributed to you and the army refused to give you the weapons, supply you with those weapons? Wasn't that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first demonstrations in front of the Knin Corps took place in January 1991 and with respect to the incidents that were taking place in the Vrljika area, the fact that people were arrested by the Croatian police, the demonstrations were held in front of the Knin Corps building to block the passage between Knin and Cetinje because of the fact that a funeral was taking place to bury a person who had died under strange circumstances. He was killed in Sibenik but was to be buried in Cetinje. Now, what you have in mind when you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm thinking about the part of the report that we read out in private session --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understand, we're in open session now, are we? Is this a public session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, open session. So stick to what you can deal with in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am bearing in mind the fact that we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I was saying, part of the report which belongs to the documents supplied by the opposite side, a document I quoted from with respect to your activities, where mention is made of those particular activities, the ones that General Mladic reacted to, and he did so quite rightly and in conformity with the rules of service, and he endeavoured to thwart them. That's what I'm talking about, and that's what it says in the report itself, the report from the Knin Corps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several reports were quoted here by Mladic. I think that to the second army in Sarajevo that was, in 1992. I don't know what the -- the one you're thinking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So avoid going into a closed session again, let's round off this Spegelj matter. Is this a forgery, what you just saw, when Spegelj is talking about the fact that they have 80.000 men who are armed with Kalashnikov rifles and that he goes on to enumerate several more thousand officers of the army of Yugoslavia who should be killed, and that nobody should be allowed to reach the barracks alive, and so on and so forth? You saw several of these excerpts. Are they falsified material? Is it just propaganda on the part of the Federal Defence Secretariat or, as you say, my propaganda? I saw this tape when you did yourself. But quite obviously it was not a forgery of any kind. It wasn't a falsified tape. Do you still claim that it is a forgery? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we all believed in it, and I did too. We all believed that it was the truth and that there would be a great pogrom and slaughterhouse of the Serbs slaughtered by the Croatian authorities. I just said that Spegelj himself, publicly, or rather, the Croatian government, denied some of the allegations from this film, this tape. Now, whether it's a forgery or not, and the background of it and how it came into existence, I really can't say. I don't know. I just spoke about the effect it had on the Serbs in Krajina and in Knin specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the film about Spegelj, there was no mention made of Knin at all. Knin was not mentioned at all, and your assertions, your claims that in the Spegelj film it was rigged to the effect that Spegelj was threatening the Serbs in Knin is not true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether Boljkovac or Spegelj was speaking, it was a conversation between Spegelj and Boljkovac. That's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, what Mr. Milosevic said is not correct. What we played here in the courtroom was actually someone referring to Knin and that the people should be slaughtered there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't recollect that, but no doubt you can refer us to the passage. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you consider that the events at the Miljevacki Plateau and Maslenica Bridge in Rani Koperi [phoen], in Peruca, Zemunik, Borovo Selo, the Medak pocket, Gospic, Pakrac, Petrinja, Vukovar, and then the Storm and Flash Operations, were they forgeries too, or, as you are saying, for the most part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not a sensible question. How can they be forgeries? It's no good running together a series of events and then trying to ask a question about them. Rephrase that in relation to one particular matter. What do you want to ask the witness? And then we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I want to ask him how he can claim that the Serbs in Croatia were disturbed through propaganda put out from Belgrade and not by the actual events that took place, the arrests that took place, the killings that took place, the discrimination, the dismissal from jobs, the pressures exerted on the them, and everything that happened to them under the impact of the new Croatian authorities from the moment they came on the scene, and even before that, in that wave of nationalism that engulfed Croatia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs were afraid. They were afraid of the intentions of the Croatian government and the intentions, as you yourself represented them as being. Secondly, because of the incidents that you implemented and the counterreaction on the part of the Croatian government to those events and the war that you waged, and the fear for reprisals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now. It's after a quarter past. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a small administrative matter. The witness lists served last week has had to be changed to a limited degree because of witnesses not being available, so there will be a further letter available for the accused by the close of this morning's session. It's going to be very helpful to us to know whether there's going to be any time for witnesses on Friday, and the earlier we can know that, the better we can plan to ensure that your time is fully used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. We'll adjourn now, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume we are in open session, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your interview with the investigators, you emphasised several times that you were making your own free interpretations. I was able to see this from the tapes that were played. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was answering questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you say you are making free interpretations, does that mean that you don't remember everything with precision? Because you were testifying about events that took place 12 years ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was saying things that I remembered with precision, and also my views of events in retrospect, from a distance. But I was expected primarily to speak about things I remember from those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You claim that I was in command of the Yugoslav People's Army, and do you know who was the Supreme Commander of the Yugoslav People's Army in 1990 and 1991? And then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In formal and legal terms, it -- the supreme commander should have been the Presidency of the SFRY. However, I understood that as of July 1991, you took over the Supreme Command over the Yugoslav People's Army and that you were in command of it through the Presidency, the Rump Presidency of Yugoslavia, and I had information that you had direct contacts with the General Staff, the Generals Kadijevic and Jovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Generals Kadijevic and Jovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I meant Adzic, Kadijevic and Adzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that before I took over my post there was a command staff of the army which reached these high ranks of generals and colonels and who constituted this top leadership of the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This entire structure that you are referring to was established before I came into office.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, General Kadijevic, in 1990, was the Federal Secretary for National Defence, and in 1991, I know that General Adzic was Chief of Staff of the JNA. The President of the Presidency, Borisav Jovic, he was in office until May 1991. Cedo Bajramovic, I think, was elected --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We don't have to be so specific about those dates.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Kostic was elected to the Presidency at the end of May 1991. So those were the men who, as of May 1991, that is, Branko Kostic, Borisav Jovic, Nedo Bajramovic, and Jugoslav Kostic were members of the Presidency of Yugoslavia. And as of October 1991, they became the Rump Presidency because certain members did not take part in the work of the Presidency. Members of the Presidency from other republics did not take part. So together with you, that was the Supreme Command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that when those military districts were formed in Yugoslavia, there was a total of four strategic groups, or army districts, the commanders in three of them were Croats: General Spegelj, General Lukasic [phoen], General Grubesic, and only in one was General Avramovic a Serb, and the air force and anti-aircraft defence was also headed by a Croat, Tus. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the people I spoke about here. Who was in those positions before that, I don't know all of them. I met General Raseta the commander of the Zagreb Corps, of the Knin Corps. I know that in the Knin Corps, the commander was a Macedonian, the Chief of Staff was a Slovene, the head of artillery was a Croat. But in the course of the summer of 1991, Serbs took over all those positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that from the moment of the armed secession in Slovenia and Croatia, the commander of the military district in Zagreb, whose area of responsibility covered Slovenia and most of Croatia and part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the general in charge was Konrad Kolsek?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from the media that that was his position. But I know of General Raseta, who I don't know whether he was a deputy or was in the staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the command of the military district. At the same time, command of the 1st Military District in Belgrade, the largest military district, was headed by a Macedonian, Aleksandar Spirkovski?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that General Spekovski was commander in Knin for a while, and later he took up duty in Belgrade. Which, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the commander of the air force and the anti-aircraft defence after General Tus, another Croat took over, Colonel Zvonko Jurjevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of those two generals from the media. I don't know the exact time periods when they were in office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Kadijevic, Brovet and Adzic, and the others that you listed, were not cadres from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from stories that General Kadijevic came -- was a native of Imotski, and General Adzic from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it then logical and normal to conclude that I was not the one who was appointing these people to leading positions of the Yugoslav People's Army, as it was still at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me in July 1991 where you should deploy the army. You asked me where you should deploy it. So you were speaking as if you were the commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can say that whatever you like as being the truth, but I'm saying that that is not true. And there are a whole series of positions in the army held by people who took over those positions before I was elected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to stop you. The witness has Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. given his evidence. You contradict it. You claim that it's not right. Now, there's no point going over the evidence to try and establish your point. You can call evidence in due course, but it will be for the Trial Chamber to determine where the truth lies. There's little point arguing whether he's telling the truth or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true that as early as 1990 -- is it true that as early as 1990, the president of the Presidency was a Slovene, Janez Drnovsek?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 15th of May, 1990, I think it was Drnovsek who was president of the Presidency. I know from the media reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1990 and 1991, when you say I was in command of the army, there was a presidency headed, in addition to Drnovsek, for a time by Stipe Mesic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From May 1990 until the end of May - I don't know the exact date, whether it was May or June 1991 - the president of the Presidency was Borisav Jovic, and after the crisis over the election of the president of the Presidency, it was Stipe Mesic, until the autumn. I don't know exactly until when, the autumn of 1991, when he ceased to be that, or rather, when Croatia became independent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well then, do you know that there was a Federal Secretary for National Defence who was Veljko Kadijevic in that period, who was also a cadre from Croatia in the top army leadership at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. I met him personally, at the end of November, maybe December, in 1991, when he said that the JNA, in connection with Vance's plan regarding withdrawal from Croatia, that the JNA would comply with the political decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he told you what was right. And do you know that in the course of the whole of 1991, they were major provocations and mistreatment of individuals, units, and facilities of the JNA in Croatia? So I'm not talking exclusively about Krajina. I'm talking about the whole of Croatia now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crisis started in January 1991, after the SFRY Presidency had taken a decision on the disarming of paramilitary units in Croatia and after the Spegelj affair was revealed and broadcast by the media, arrests started. The JNA, or rather, the institutions, the competent institutions of the JNA, would issue indictments and start proceedings against individual officials of the government of Croatia. I think two of them were put on trial, but Spegelj was not accessible. And from that moment on, demonstrations started in Croatia against the JNA. Later on there were blockages of barracks, and in August an open war started between the JNA and armed formations of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of the attempts of the Presidency of SFRY to halt the escalation, for example, at a meeting on the 22nd of July, that was also attended by Tudjman, the demand was made to cease all hostilities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a cessation of hostilities had been agreed on, that a commission was formed, headed by Branko Kostic, and that commission, and members of that commission would go to Croatia, to Krajina, and to Slovenia to insist on respect for the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the first serious conflict between JNA units and National Guards occurred in Dalj on the 1st of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was fighting in Dalj. Exactly who was there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The National Guards, were they a paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The National Guards Corps, the ZNG, were an armed formation of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that Vladimir Seks, president of the Crisis Staff for Eastern Slavonia and Baranja in August 1991 informed the public that units of the JNA would no longer be supplied with electricity, water, food, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of those events. And it wasn't just Seks who spoke about that, but others as well. Others were saying that too, from the Croatian authorities, and that is what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that military facilities and units were constantly exposed to armed provocations and attacks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First there was a blockade, and I'm not aware of the situation with all the facilities, but I do know that the JNA facilities were blocked in Sibenik, Zadar, Sinj, Split. There were media reports about the events in Varazdin, Bjelovar, then also there were television reports over demonstrations and blockades of the barracks in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned a series of towns all over Croatia, and was it obvious that the suspension of supplies for barracks and other military facilities and constant attacks called in question the very physical survival of members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a blockade. What the exact situation was inside the barracks, I don't know, but I do know that they were blocked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that JNA units were forced to break through, to get out of that blockade, and to respond to such attacks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, some JNA units undertook to deblock those garrisons, as in Zadar, for example. The deblocking of the garrison in Sibenik, and the JNA would announce those actions taken against the Croatian guards, and they were explained by the need to deblock those barracks. But I don't know exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that the explanation that it was essential to deblock the garrisons that were blocked was a correct explanation, or was it a fabricated one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the explanation of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that finally in November 1991, when all those barracks all over Croatia were blocked, and when clashes broke out, an agreement was signed in Igalo on the cessation of hostilities and on the need for all sides to cease all armed actions of all kinds for people to be able to sit around a table and find a peaceful solution, in the presence of Lord Carrington, in November 1991, in Igalo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were many agreements on the cessation of hostilities. The last, I suppose, was agreed in Sarajevo, and you took part in some of those, I think the agreement in Geneva, which was mentioned in those days, and your approval of the Vance Plan. That also implied a cessation of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the agreement in November occurred prior to these questions that we have discussed the link to the Vance Plan. I should now like to play an audio cassette which you call an intercepted conversation, simply for you to see to what extent it confirms how correct what I am saying is. It is in the technical booth. Could it be played please. It is a conversation between the then Croatian president Franjo Tudjman and the Federal Secretary for National Defence, General Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid the interpreters do not have a text and the sound is very bad. [Voiceover] They're always looking for a way of blaming others for what he has done. Can peace be established or not? If it can be stopped until 10 hours, and secondly, if the military barracks can be deblocked and everything else by 12.00, if that is done, then after that we can continue what we have started. If that cannot be done, then the two of us will no longer hear one another. We'll not be in contact any more. You know what we should perhaps do? Maybe we should try that -- before we get together by fax to confirm, because of Croatia, a written truce, which means an agreement that would deal with the army in the way that suits the sovereign Croatian authorities and it's also in the interest of the army. Does that mean, Franjo, that you put what is second in first place and vice versa? No. We have agreed with Carrington on the order of things. If we haven't let stop -- discontinue any further conversation. What if we are unable to achieve that? What do you mean if we're not able to achieve that? If in Sibenik things worsen. I can guarantee that not a single bullet will be fired. We have the deadline up to 10.00, 1000 hours. Let fire be ceased, deblocking by 12.00. We will continue this conversation tomorrow. A solution must be found. If you agree. If you are not capable of doing that, say so. It's up to you. Then everyone will go back to his own positions and we'll see what will happen. Then there will be a disaster. Of course there will. I'm doing this for the last time, for the last time, with the great responsibility that I bear, and you also have that responsibility. The worst should be avoided. You can avoid it by fulfilling each of these points. Today is the turning point. I will do as much as I can. Stop these developments in Sibenik. Cease fire everywhere and let the troops get water and food and everything they need, and tomorrow we can sit at a table and talk openly about everything. Otherwise we'll go back to hostilities. I think that is a disaster. But I'm sure a solution can be found. If I didn't believe that, I wouldn't be talking to you in this way. And I believe that you are doing the same. Let's try. That would be disastrous. Stop the fire in Sibenik by 1000 hours. Order a ceasefire. If you're not capable of doing that -- if Letica is working over there, he's worse than that Spegelj. You must do something about it. We'll see. I didn't mention Grubesic as well. It's Grubesic, not Letica. Grubesic is not Letica. He -- when he left, I knew that he wouldn't come back. That is up to him. You conclude from that that this is generalised -- these feelings are generalised. Well, if that is so, then go to war. I'm just asking for a ceasefire, nothing more. What we have already signed, that's all. I'm going to act along those lines. But you think of whether there's a way of getting out of this hell. There must be an absolute ceasefire by 1000 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hours, absolute ceasefire, so that people can live. You must -- they must be given water. They have to live. Would you let them die in that way? And this thing that Anto Markovic is preparing, it's very dangerous, this business. He's a son of a bitch that you know well. I've told you that many times. Get hold of these two and then we've solved everything. Because he wasn't there when the signature was required, because no one is -- has any respect for him anyway. Okay. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment, Mr. Milosevic. First of all, our thanks to the interpreters for managing. Very difficult. Now, that's not a tape which has been produced so far, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, would you like that tape exhibited? You've had it played. Very well. The next number, and we will order a transcript for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Defence Exhibit 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no doubt that the conversation was conducted after a meeting and the signing of an agreement on a cessation of hostilities with Lord Carrington. There is also no doubt, this is indisputable, isn't it, Mr. MILAN BABIC?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take part in that agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Is it also clear that the conversation is being conducted in connection with the generalised blockade of JNA barracks in Croatia and that it relates to relationships between Croatia and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the conversation, one could conclude that they were referring to the blockade of barracks, specifically, the one in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were also talking about other barracks, about the blocking of barracks, about the fact that they are being cut off by refusing them water and other supplies, and the request, as you can see, was made by General Kadijevic only to respect the agreement made with the old, wise Lord Carrington, as he put it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the contents of the conversation we heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it then clear from this that General Kadijevic insists that any solution is wiser than war, insisting that his barracks be deblocked? Did you hear him say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard Kadijevic say so on the tape, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear Kadijevic guarantee that not a single bullet would be fired if they would only stop shooting at the army? Did you hear him say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it on the tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear him say: Once you stop, once we sign a ceasefire, we'll sit around a table? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who is working for a cessation of hostilities and for peace there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know specifically about events related to the lifting of the blockade of the barracks in Zadar from General Vukovic. I heard from him about the way he accomplished that and his signing of an agreement with the authorities in Zadar and the pulling out of troops from that barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about the number of times that troops were being shot at while being pulled out of their barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never heard of Sarajevo, Tuzla, about any other place in Bosnia, when troops leaving in an orderly fashion their barracks, being shot at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard two things in media reports. One concerned a blockade of a convoy of military equipment that was blocked by Croatian authorities, and I heard about events in Sarajevo, when the staff of the 2nd Army was leaving. I was told that by General Kukanjac, who spoke about that on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about these other events, from the times which you mention, calling it testimony. Is it true that in that period, in 1990 and 1991, the president -- or rather, the Prime Minister of Yugoslavia was Ante Markovic, a Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that Veljko Kadijevic, whom we heard on tape, was Minister of Defence in his government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Kadijevic was Federal Secretary of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1992 the Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established, was Milan Panic, my opponent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was talk in the media and in the public that you appointed him to that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you know, he was my political opponent, that he was supported by the then president of the SFRY, that he was also my rival at elections for the president of Serbia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to statements one could hear at the time, he was advocating peace, and that was the point of conflict between you and him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us then stick to what you say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that at that time in the media and from rumours. I have no personal, direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't see how anyone can talk about something that they have no personal knowledge about. I'm now asking you about various positions held within the Yugoslav government: Minister of Defence, Prime Minister, et cetera. What is the connection, then, of Serbia with the military legislation, with rules of procedure, with transfers of people from one place to another? You even brought here, as some kind of document, a paper referring to a woman from your bureau being allocated for temporary employment in a military-medical section, probably to keep records about refugees, the wounded from Krajina. What has that got to do with decision-making in Serbia, the transfer of some woman from your bureau to the military medical academy, an army medical institution, and God knows what else you brought here among those papers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two things I want to say, beginning with July 1991. I realised, and you told me, that you are the Supreme Command of the JNA, and the staff of the Supreme Command consisted of the General Staff and the Defence Secretary. And you were also member of the supreme military council of the FRY and the de facto leader of that council. In addition to Zoran Lilic, who was your yes-man. I don't know how long Bulatovic was a figure there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when you replaced him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when Lilic became president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After you replaced Dobrica Cosic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that it was in 1993 that he assumed this position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's when you replaced Dobrica Cosic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the replacement of Dobrica Cosic. I'm telling you that Lilic became president of the FRY in 1993 and that his term of office was until midsummer 1997, for four years.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Dobrica Cosic was president until mid-1993, this yes-man of mine that you mentioned. All these events that you're testifying to happened before 1993, wherein I am the commander of the army, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me a question from the period when the SFRY existed and some questions about FRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was asking you about things from 1990, 1991, until 1993. When was I commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You commanded from July 1991, using your personal clout over the General Staff --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judging by what you say, it was I who explained to you that I have influence over the General Staff. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked several questions. In fact, you noted several things first, one of them being: Until July 1991, although it was also in 1990, that you were saying that you would protect us, that JNA would protect our right to stay within Yugoslavia and guarantee that right of ours. In July 1991, you came forward with a question: Where should you deploy the army? That means that from that moment on, you showed that you were able to command the army and that you were commanding it, as of that moment. As for the Presidency of Yugoslavia, it was partly disabled, that is, the Presidency was normally made up of eight members, and starting with October there were only four left. The JNA got involved in military actions, or rather, started the war in Croatia, in October, and until then, on orders from the Presidency, or even only on the initiative of Borisav Jovic, because he said the JNA, as decided by him, got involved in Pakrac. Anyway, as of July, together with Kostic, Cedo Bajramovic, you were the commander of the JNA, and Veljko Kadijevic and Adzic were the men whom you controlled in the General Staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MILAN BABIC, you know for how long this Presidency was disabled, precisely because four members voted always against the other four members, and they were never able to make a decision.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Presidency made a decision to introduce a state of immediate threat of war. I don't know how many members were active at that time, but it was made in October 1991. And that decision was followed by adoption of some new rules that enabled the remaining four members to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. command the army in the absence of the other four, and you were the boss of the remaining four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that it was a time when Yugoslavia was being exhausted and tortured under the pressure of great powers, and as for your claim that I commanded the army, I wish I had. We would have been able to avoid the war.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were the one deploying the JNA troops as of October 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to intervene to say this: We've been over this point really for some time. The witness has explained why he has come to the conclusion which he did, and it will be for us to determine on the evidence. Now, I don't think we should spend more time going over the same point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that your explanations, judging from the tape of your interviews with investigators and the lady on the opposite side, explanations related to the appointment of General Mrksic, as commander of the Serbian army of Krajina, these explanations would very graphically show how riddled with contradictions they are with your own personal statements and with other facts as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want to put a specific point, you can. It sounds as though it's a point which should be put in private session. But you can't make generalisations of the sort so far that you are making. If you want to make a specific point about this, it sounds as though we should go into private session. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the point that you want to make to the witness? Because so far it's so generalised, it's not to be worth very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, are we in private session now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're in private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, during examination-in-chief, the witness told us one version of the alleged meeting he had with me, related to his request for a new commander of the Serbian army of Krajina. You will now see the first version, which is brief, and you will then see the second version, also his, and we'll see how it actually happened, and then I'll ask him some questions. I would kindly ask you to play that tape. It is your own tape from the interview with MILAN BABIC, when he speaks of a meeting with me, when Prime Minister Mikelic attended, he and Minister of Foreign Affairs, none of them being competent to discuss the issues at hand, and he came to me to request a new commander of the Serbian army of Krajina, and you will see what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we please have the date of the tape so that we can find the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see if we can --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19th February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let us have the passage played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "MILAN BABIC ... took place. I have no assertions concerning this. I would like to give this my free interpretation. So Mikelic had prepared an information on the situation. He prepared a speech. Then he read out this lengthy speech, study. I don't know -- I cannot remember exactly what he read out, because he was always very lengthy, went into great detail. Nor do I remember exactly what he concretely said in that speech of his. But what I do remember is the following scene: At a certain point, Milosevic said, "Wait a minute, please," and he moved to the other room, where his desk is, and to the inner office. And he stayed there a short time, I believe, probably a minute, a couple of minutes. So he went out and he was absent a few minutes. And he came back and he said, more or less, 'The new commander will be Mile Mrksic.' Now, some two or three years ago I talked about this event with [redacted]. "MR. HARDIN: Before you go into that, let's finish first with what was said in the meeting. "MILAN BABIC: Well, this is in connection with the meeting, but ... "MR. HARDIN: I know, but I mean within the meeting itself. What else was said in the meeting? "MILAN BABIC: I don't remember anything in particular. So I remember that when we were going out, exiting, there was Goran Hadzic, and I think he was there at that meeting. And I think it was on that occasion, because there was no other such occasion that I could have witnessed it. He said, 'Mr.. President, can I remain with you, the two of us alone, for a short while?' Then we went out in the hall. He stayed there a short time and then he came out after us. That is what I remember of that scene and that meeting. "MR. HARDIN: Okay. Do you know if Milosevic mentioned during the meeting -- had he talked to anybody about the selection of Mrksic? "MILAN BABIC: This is what I wanted to say. "MR. HARDIN: Okay. Just a minute. Okay. Okay. Just a minute. "MILAN BABIC: I don't remember whether he said it. "MR. HARDIN: Okay. Subsequent to the meeting, did Mile Mrksic become the commander? "MILAN BABIC: Yes. The Assembly approved his appointment at the end of May of that year. I don't remember what the exact proceeding, procedure was, but he did become the commander. "MR. HARDIN: Okay. Go ahead. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Let me ask: Why were you there? You are not involved with military. Why were you there? "MILAN BABIC: No. I was the Minister of Foreign Affairs. Mikelic formed the delegation. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Did you run the delegation when you were there? Did you have your own proposal who you wanted to be the commander? "MILAN BABIC: Personally, no, but -- and I don't remember that any one of us spoke about that. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Did you -- did any of you, when Mr. Milosevic said he, this guy Mile Mrksic, is the commander, did anyone respond to that? Did you say either say, 'Well, great,' or did you oppose it? [Inaudible]. "MILAN BABIC: I don't remember. Probably no. I don't know. I can't remember when and where, but it was after this meeting that somewhere Martic told me. It was after this meeting. I was in some company, with people. I can't remember [inaudible] that Jovica Stanisic went and had a talk with General Celeketic. I remember that I heard this. Somebody conveyed it to me. This was a piece of information which remains something interesting to me, and that's why I remember it, but I cannot remember under what circumstances I heard that. "MR. HARDIN: When you guys went to the meeting with Mikelic, did he make a proposal for someone to be the commander? "MILAN BABIC: I couldn't -- I cannot remember. "MR. HARDIN: You don't recall if any names were discussed? "MILAN BABIC: No, I don't think that any names were being discussed. Well ... "THE INTERPRETER: Could you ask him to repeat that? "MR. HARDIN: Yes. You need to repeat. "MILAN BABIC: Yes. [redacted] [redacted], about this event, he mentioned that the Supreme Defence -- that Milosevic mentioned that the Supreme Defence Council has -- had chosen, had appointed this man. And he probably thought of the Supreme Defence Council of Yugoslavia, that he was there, that it was agreed that Mrksic become the commander, but I personally do not recall that. "MR. HARDIN: Okay. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Is Mrksic from the Krajina? "MILAN BABIC: It was said that he was -- he had his roots in Kordun. Whether he was born in Kordun or whether his -- the previous generations came from Kordun --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can go on. You have the tape, and I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We need to finish the topic. [Videotape played]. MILAN BABIC: Yes. That is what was said, that he's a member of the JNA. I cannot remember whether that was being said then or later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The army of the Krajina, didn't they have any candidate that could fulfil this position? MILAN BABIC: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this -- MILAN BABIC: Well, the Supreme Council of Defence of Krajina could probably discuss that, but whether they discussed it or not, I do not know, and I was not a member of this body.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this General Celeketic, was he also a member of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That seems to be moving on to another topic. We'll finish it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll come back to this topic, but I think that the questions which I am able to ask this witness in connection to the tape can be asked in open session, because they -- the audience can't see the tape. So can I ask my questions in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It depends whether you can ask them without referring to the tape, since the tape has been played in private session, any reference to it or anything referring to his responses, possibly need playing. Let me consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. On reflection, there's no secrecy about the fact that there was an interview, as I recollect. The only matter which is secret is the identity of the witness, and therefore, that was the reason that the tapes were played in private session. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, that's right, isn't it? There's no reason why the questions about the content of the interview can't be asked in open session, provided they don't identify the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what also should not be identified is that it was a suspect interview, because that was discussed in private session, that it was a suspect interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it can be referred to as an interview with the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Milosevic, you get that? So no reference to -- which might identify him, and it can only be referred to as an interview with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to refer back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, but just refer to it as an interview. Don't describe it any more fully. So that what you can't say is that it was a suspect interview. That's the point. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yes. Let's go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it clear from the tape that has been played, from this interview, that the delegation, or rather, the members of the delegation, its structure, was not in conformity with the alleged subject that you were alluding to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prime Minister was a member of the supreme council of defence of Krajina, and you couldn't see this on the tape, but he had his own proposal as to the command of the Serbian army of the RSK, Milan Novakovic was mentioned, but very briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you now. Please answer my questions and we'll get to that. We'll come to that part of the tape in due course to see the contradictions that you stated in respect of what you're saying. Did you happen to note, to notice, that you yourself speak about a long speech made by your head of delegation, which was made up in the way it was? Isn't that right? There was a long address made by him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you couldn't remember to what it referred, to what it was all about, but that you assumed that he touched upon many vital issues for the economic, political, public life of Krajina, and cooperation with Serbia, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, the priorities discussed were the events in Western Slavonia, the Croatian Flash operation, the exodus of the population, the question of the army, of the RSK, to stand up to the Croatian army. So at that time, those were the main topics discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said a moment ago that you can't remember at all what was said in, as you termed it, the very long speech made by the head of your delegation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what the priorities were of the discussions at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you consider those to be priorities indirectly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that was the only specific topic discussed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, is it clear from the interview that you asked me a question, and that question was whether I knew anything about the newly appointed commander of the Serbian army of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you asked whether I knew who was going to be appointed, because it didn't come under your competency. I assume it was the competency of the President of the Republic, or rather, your Supreme Defence Council and the president of your republic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, linked to that event, in his presentation, the Prime Minister mentioned one name, and that was the name of General Mile Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I'm asking you about your own interview. In the whole of your interview, you never said that. You never stated that. What you said was that I told you to wait and that I went into my office to speak over the telephone, which means I went to ask, I went to inquire of somebody who was supposed to know about those matters.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what my knowledge was in concrete terms about the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I told you to wait. I went into my office to ask and inquire, because you had asked me something that I wasn't able to answer myself at that point, so I went to inquire.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had determined that General Mile Mrksic should be the new commander of the RSK army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you drew that conclusion yourself, your interview speaks otherwise. But let's move on to the next question. In the interview, did you happen to notice that you were first asked by the lady sitting opposite whether you had a proposal to make of any kind? Isn't that right? And your answer was that you did not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't remember everything on that occasion and all the details at that particular point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm just talking about what we all had occasion to see a moment ago. Then the investigator went on to ask you whether you had discussed any of the proposals before the meeting, and your answer there again was no, that you did not, that you had not. And then once again the lady opposite went on to ask you: Did you not have in Krajina somebody who could be put forward as a candidate? And your answer to that question too was no; no, you did not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You said you didn't know. So you were asked three times in the course of the interview whether you had a candidate, whether you discussed a candidate, whether any names were mentioned; and your answer to all three questions was that you did not remember, that you do not know, and that no names were mentioned, that you don't know if there was a candidate or not, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remembered the names subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that. We'll come that part of the tape where you remembered and the circumstances under which you remembered, but that's another matter for the moment. Then you go on to say that you heard from - I don't want to identify the person. I suppose that is not allowed either - that this took place at the Supreme Defence Council for the defence of Yugoslavia. Well, all right. At that Supreme Defence Council meeting, in view of the fact that I'm a member of the Supreme Defence Council, would we be able to assume that I know about that and that I don't have to go and tell you: Wait a moment, for me to go and ring somebody up and inquire and then come back to you and give you an answer as to what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was what the witness said happened. Now, explanations you can give in due course, if you want. But assist us with this: In that part of the interview, there was no mention of Novakovic; rather, you said there wasn't a candidate. Now, if you want to give an explanation of why you said that, you should be able to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He will have an opportunity of -- Mr. May, to save time, I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to show you a part of the tape on which you will see how this actually happened. So I do have an answer for you, on the basis of what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him give his explanation now. The matter is being put to him. He should be entitled to answer. Yes. Can you give us -- if you want to, give a brief explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment when I was asked, I didn't remember all the details. I just remembered the main event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we able to conclude, therefore, that in that interview you were asked three times: Twice by the lady sitting opposite and once by the investigator, whether you had a proposal, whether any proposal was discussed, whether it was possible that there was no solution in Krajina itself, suitable solution, but that you had to go to Belgrade; and to all those questions your answer was negative: No, no, and I don't remember?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in the structures that decided on issues at that time, at that stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't afterwards either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't even know whether Mrksic was from Krajina. You said that he might have been born there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People said that he was born in Kordun, that his origins were in Kordun. What that meant -- whether he was born there or his parents were born there, I don't know what that means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
