utterances.text: Well, I originated from Pozarevac, which means I was born in Pozarevac, and not that some of my people were born in Pozarevac. I am a native of Pozarevac, which means I was born there. Now, do you know that he was born in Vrginmost, or rather, the Vrginmost municipality, that he completed elementary school there and indeed secondary school as well, on that territory, and that he only left the Republic of Croatia when he enrolled in the military academy, like anybody else who enrolls in the military academy, because the academy is located in Belgrade? At least it was in Yugoslavia, in the Yugoslavia of the day, the one in which Mrksic lived. So not only was he a native of the area, but he lived there right up until the time when he left to attend his higher education at the military academy, and that was the profession he had chosen. He was a man from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't know about those details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, fine. You didn't know those details, but you do know the other details that you cannot recollect. Now, the second part of this same conversation held on the same day, but I do wish to draw your attention to the fact that you will see at the very beginning that a different story is being told now, after a break for lunch and after the witness was warned that he hadn't done his homework properly and now he has to tell a different story. So we'll now hear that different story after the instructor gave him instructions as to how he should tell that story. So please play that second excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll certainly do that. We'll come back to any allegations that you are making and explore what they are. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And I would like to object against this way that he actually indicates there was an instructor telling him what he has to tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He can put it to the witness in due course. Yes, a matter for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge May, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let's play the tape. The witness, in due course -- private session. The witness, in due course, can deal with these allegations that are being made.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "MR. HARDIN: The time is approximately 1422 --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please -- I apologise for the interruption. Will you stop, please. I asked you to start this second clip from 1249, 12 hours, 49 minutes, please, and not 1422 minutes, as it says on the tape. You have the time indicated in the top left-hand corner. From 1249, please. It is indicative of what I am saying and claiming, and it takes very little time, because in the meantime there was a lunch break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand why this is taking so long. It was just a minute prior to what was played a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "MR. HARDIN: The time right now is approximately 1422, on the 19th of February. We just had a lunch break. And Mr. Babic, I need to remind you of your warnings again. Do you have any questions about your warnings? "MILAN BABIC: No. "MR. HARDIN: Okay. All right. I will move on to the area of Western Slavonia. "MR. MUELLER: Let him make a short remark, please, he's going to make a short remark. "MR. HARDIN: Apparently you wanted to say something, according to Mr. Mueller. "MR. MUELLER: But short, but short, please. "MILAN BABIC: Yes, in reference to our previous talks concerning my meetings with Mr. Milosevic. And when I spoke of that meeting in May 1995 with Milosevic, I remembered, in connection with one of your questions, whether the people from -- the members of the delegation from Krajina, whether they have any proposals, names for a new commander of the army of Serbian Krajina, I remember, I recollect, and I can answer yes, there was this proposal. Borislav Mikelic asked that the newly appointed commander be Mile Novakovic, General Mile Novakovic. Then Milosevic made a negative comment in connection with this person and stopped this discussion. Secondly, what I would like to add --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll stop the playing. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You've got a minute or two more, and then if you're going to suggest that this witness has been instructed in some way, you must do so. And we'll go back into open session. We are in open --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this interview, do we see that there was a lunch break after a certain period of time and that after that lunch break the investigator asks his collocutor, in this case Witness Croat MILAN BABIC, whether he has anything to add, and he says that he hasn't? And then we see his representative, attorney, telling him - his legal representative - that he has something to say, that he has forgotten to say something. I don't want to mention the name of his legal representative, as this is the only witness we have had so far with an attorney sitting in the courtroom while he's testifying. And then he makes a statement that he has remembered. So during the lunch break he remembered something that he answered three times in the negative, that he didn't know and that couldn't remember, that he suddenly remembered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've just seen all of this. Why don't you come to the point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point is that those two statements are in complete contradiction with one another, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question is: How did the witness come to make the second statement? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume, and I'm asking him: Did that happen because in the meantime he was advised and cautioned that he hadn't said what had been planned for him to say and that he hadn't answered three questions - two put by the lady opposite and one by the investigator - that he had answered no, but really he should have said yes, and he should have offered, proffered, a name which now his legal representative had to remind him to give that name after the lunch break. So he is correcting himself because suddenly his memory has been refreshed, so he now has a completely different story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer the question. Let the witness answer what's being put to him. You've heard what's being suggested now, Witness, and you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the investigator asked me whether I had anything to add regarding the rights that were read to me. It was in that connection. That is one thing. Secondly, the answer that I had something to add in addition to what was previously discussed was correct. Because my first reaction was a visual picture of the incident. I have a very good visual memory, and I recounted on the basis of that visual memory. Then I thought about the event and remembered some other details in connection with it, and that is what I added after the break. There was no pressure, there was no suggestions as to what I should say; only what I really remembered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as this tape is concerned, and there are any number of tapes of this kind, that they could be used as evidence for false testimony on the part of not only this witness but obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've heard the answer. There's no question of that. You've heard his answer. It's something he remembered. Now, time has come for us to adjourn. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, if the accused wishes, arrangements should be made for those extracts, at least to be exhibited so the Court has them before it. We seem to have them already. Mr. Milosevic, do you want us to have these extracts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm being told it's D57. The only point that I make about that - and you may want to consider this - is D57 is a particular exhibit relating to a particular date, whether it would be more sensible to go on to D57A perhaps for this one. Yes, we'll make that D57A.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. May. But I would also like to request from you that you institute proceedings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as there are grounds to believe that this is false testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We hear what you say, but you've heard what the witness has said. He's given his explanation. Now, it will be a matter for us to determine whether the explanation holds water or not. Certainly no question of any proceedings or anything of that sort. Thank you very much. We've now got this passage exhibited, D57A, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Your Honour, just to add: It's only the first part, because the second part we just heard, and we supply tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That part can be added to D57A, since it's all the same interview. We are, as I say, going to adjourn now. Before we do, one or two administrative matters. Mr. Tapuskovic, if you have any questions -- I don't know if -- do you have any questions of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had intended to raise that matter tomorrow morning and to tell you that this time I would really like to ask to have time -- of course, it is up to you to decide, but it seems to me that in this case I should not be put in a position - even though I do my very best to select only the matters of professional importance - that I be spared of being rushed. I don't know exactly how much time I would need, but I think I need at least one-third of one day, of one working day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we're talking about an hour and a quarter, something of that sort; is that right? Seventy-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would do my best to complete it within that time limit, but I really do think that in view of the significance of this testimony, I should be allowed that much time, maybe a couple of minutes more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that in due course. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we think the Prosecution should have another witness available for Friday. We would ask you, too, to bear in mind, having regard to the length of this witness's evidence, the length of your re-examination, and keep it, if you would, to the bearest minimum.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I will do so, and I think at the moment it will not be longer than half an hour, probably less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the sort of time which we had in mind. Thank you. Very well. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
